articles.title: Subnetting and CIDR Notation: A Practical Guide
articles.excerpt: Working out whether 192.168.1.130 is on the same network as 192.168.1.73/26 should take a few seconds. Guess wrong and you end up with a VPN range that swallows your LAN, or a firewall rule that match…
articles.body: Working out whether 192.168.1.130 is on the same network as 192.168.1.73/26 should take a few seconds. Guess wrong and you end up with a VPN range that swallows your LAN, or a firewall rule that matches far more than you meant. This guide shows how CIDR notation maps to bits, how to find network and broadcast addresses by hand, how to carve a /24 into subnets for a home lab, and how to check what your Linux hosts are configured with. Bits, prefixes, and masks An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number. Dotted-quad notation splits it into four 8-bit octets and writes each one in decimal, so every octet runs from 0 to 255. 192 .168 .1 .73 11000000 10101000 00000001 01001001 The prefix length after the slash says how many of those 32 bits, counted from the left, identify the network.

articles.title: The Agent Added a Second Copy of a Utility the Repo Already Had
articles.excerpt: Quick answer: When an agent adds a "small helper" that already exists elsewhere in the repo, you don't just have a duplicate file. You now have two functions that look identical today but will drift a…
articles.body: Quick answer: When an agent adds a "small helper" that already exists elsewhere in the repo, you don't just have a duplicate file. You now have two functions that look identical today but will drift apart the first time someone fixes a bug in one of them. Treat the discovery of an existing utility as a hard stop: reuse it, or deliberately consolidate, never silently fork it. I found the pattern on a routine review of a checkout change. The agent had introduced formatMoneyCents() in a new pricing.ts . It was well written, it had a unit test, and the feature worked.

articles.title: The eMudhra fix lives in your Go binary, not in your Docker image
articles.excerpt: On October 19, Go shipped two security releases: 1.27.3 and 1.26.10. The fix touches a single package, crypto/x509. I rebuilt one of my Go services on the same Docker image as before. Go's own scanner…
articles.body: On October 19, Go shipped two security releases: 1.27.3 and 1.26.10. The fix touches a single package, crypto/x509 . I rebuilt one of my Go services on the same Docker image as before. Go's own scanner still found the flaw. TL;DR : the eMudhra fix is a list of eight banned keys, written into the code of crypto/x509 . That list is compiled into your binary. Updating the base image or the system certificates does not add it. You have to rebuild with Go 1.27.3 or 1.26.10, then redeploy. If your Dockerfile still builds with Go 1.25, rebuilding changes nothing: that version gets no more fixes. Versions and source status: snapshot as of October 31, 2026. Check the latest fixes before deploying. This article is for Go developers and for teams that ship Go services in containers.

articles.excerpt: Plausible's 9,526 title matches cross public dashboards and Stats API keys Plausible Analytics is designed to make website statistics easy to share and query. That flexibility creates several access p…
articles.body: Plausible's 9,526 title matches cross public dashboards and Stats API keys Plausible Analytics is designed to make website statistics easy to share and query. That flexibility creates several access paths: the private team dashboard, public or shared dashboard links, the Stats API, and the Sites API used to manage sites. A count of Plausible-looking pages is therefore not a count of private analytics accounts. A ZoomEye SDK count-only query on November 2, 2026 returned 0 matches for app="Plausible" and 9,526 for title="Plausible" with sub_type=all , page 1, and page size 1. A combined title="Plausible" && http.body="Plausible" query returned 9,257. The body-only count was 278,024, which is too broad to support a product claim.

articles.title: Planetary defense: How military and civil satellites are watching fireballs to help keep Earth safe from space rocks
articles.excerpt: Satellites are watching fireballs blaze through Earth's atmosphere, strengthening planetary defense knowhow and helping scientists learn more about space debris impacts.
articles.body: It came from outer space, exploding high above the South Atlantic off the coast of Argentina. That April 1 event — an incoming meteor , also termed a bolide — was observed by both U.S. space-based military and civil sensors. Hush-hush U.S. government satellite sensors detected the speedy fireball cutting through our atmosphere. The object's brightness peaked at an altitude of nearly 60 miles (90.5 kilometers) over the South Atlantic. That dazzling spectacle was also caught by the National Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration's GOES-E and Europe's Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) Imager-1 satellite. Those two independent spacecraft in geostationary orbit detected the bolide via onboard lightning imagers.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 1, 1962: The Soviet Union Launches Mars 1 spacecraft to Red Planet during the Space Race
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. While it did end up flying by Mars , the mission was not exactly a success. After it separated from the rocket, it deployed its solar panels and started cruising toward Mars. When mission controllers were checking out the telemetry it transmitted back to Earth, they found out that Mars 1 had sprung a leak in one of the gas valves that controls the spacecraft's orientation. And without a working orientation system, Mars 1 would have a hard time pointing its antennas in the right direction. It lost contact with Earth when it was about halfway to Mars . A model of Mars 1, a Mars flyby spacecraft launched to the Red Planet by the Soviet Union on Nov. 1, 1962.

articles.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
articles.excerpt: It's still unknown how attackers got access to Anthropic's verified Cursor account.
articles.body: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont.
